headline: LinkedIn job offer hides backdoor in GitHub repo
summary: A developer narrowly avoided a supply chain attack disguised as a job opportunity, highlighting the growing sophistication of social engineering tactics.
details: A developer received a LinkedIn message from a recruiter for a crypto startup, offering a lead engineer role. The recruiter asked the developer to review a public GitHub repository, specifically to "check out the deprecated Node modules issue."

Instead of cloning the repository directly, the developer set up a sandboxed VPS and used a read-only agent to analyze the code. The agent quickly flagged a suspicious file, app/test/index.js, which was disguised as a test suite.

This file contained a hidden backdoor. It assembled a URL to a remote server and was configured to execute any payload sent back. The backdoor was triggered automatically by the 'prepare' script during the 'npm install' process, making it a potent supply chain attack.

The commits in the repository were falsely attributed to a legitimate developer, whose GitHub profile and personal website were used to lend credibility. The developer confirmed they had no involvement with the malicious repository.

Similarly, the recruiter's LinkedIn profile belonged to a real arts journalist. When the developer feigned installation issues, the profile persona shifted to an expert on npm and Node versions, revealing the impersonation.

The developer reported the malicious repository to GitHub and the recruiter to LinkedIn, but as of the report, the code remained active. This incident underscores the importance of extreme caution and security hygiene when handling unsolicited code reviews, especially when initiated through social media.

The FBI recently dismantled a Chinese phishing service linked to $1.9 billion in losses and millions of stolen cards, demonstrating the scale of AI-assisted cybercrime. This incident highlights how such tools are being weaponized for social engineering attacks.
